contents.html: This report summarizes the discussion at the second “Cyber AI Profile Workshop,” in January 20506 during which focused on the Preliminary Draft of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework Profile for Artificial Intelligence (Cyber AI Profile). The workshop gathered input across government, industry, and academia to provide guidance for managing cybersecurity risks associated with AI systems and for leveraging AI to enhance cybersecurity capabilities to inform the next draft of the NIST Cyber AI Profile. NIST also provided an update on its work to develop the Special Publication (SP) 800-53 Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems (COSAiS). The report highlights key themes raised during the discussions, including governance challenges, stability of the Profile over time, AI attack surfaces, the need for consistent AI taxonomy, ideas for specific risk-based guidance and resources to support usability (e.g., use cases), and AI-enabled cyber defense opportunities.
contents.html_ja: 本報告書は、2026年1月開催の2回目の「Cyber AI Profile ワークショップ」での議論をまとめたものです。このワークショップは、NIST Cybersecurity Framework Profile for Artificial Intelligence（Cyber AI Profile）の予備ドラフトに焦点を当てていました。ワークショップでは、政府、産業界、学術界から意見を集め、AI システムに関連するサイバーセキュリティリスクを管理するための指針と、サイバーセキュリティ能力を強化するために AI を活用するための指針を示し、NIST Cyber AI Profile の次のドラフトに反映させることを目指しました。NIST は、Special Publication（SP）800-53 Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems（COSAiS）の策定作業の最新状況も報告しました。本報告書は、議論で挙がった主要なテーマを取り上げています。これには、ガバナンス上の課題、Profile の長期的な安定性、AI の攻撃対象領域、一貫した AI 分類体系の必要性、特定のリスクベースの指針に関する案と使いやすさを支援するリソース（たとえば、ユースケース）、AI を活用したサイバー防御の機会が含まれます。

contents.html: The Information Technology Laboratory (ITL) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) promotes the U.S. economy and public welfare by providing technical leadership for the Nation’s measurement and standards infrastructure. ITL develops tests, test methods, reference data, proof of concept implementations, and technical analyses to advance the development and productive use of information technology. ITL’s responsibilities include the development of management, administrative, technical, and physical standards and guidelines for the cost-effective security and privacy of other than national security-related information in federal information systems.
contents.html_ja: 国立標準技術研究所（NIST）の情報技術研究所（ITL）は、国の計測・標準インフラに技術面でのリーダーシップを提供することで、米国経済と公共の福祉を促進しています。ITL は、情報技術の開発と生産的な利用を進めるために、試験、試験方法、参照データ、概念実証の実装、技術分析を開発しています。ITL の責務には、連邦情報システムにおける、国家安全保障関連以外の情報について、費用対効果の高いセキュリティとプライバシーを確保するための管理・運用・技術・物理面の標準とガイドラインの策定が含まれます。

contents.html: On January 14, 2026, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE) hosted the public workshop Cyber AI Profile Workshop #2 to gather feedback on the Preliminary Draft of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework Profile for Artificial Intelligence (Cyber AI Profile) [1] published on December 16, 2025. This document provides a summary of the workshop’s discussions, including opening remarks, panel, morning presentations, and afternoon breakout sessions. This workshop aimed to raise awareness of artificial intelligence (AI) and cybersecurity projects at NIST and obtain feedback on priority areas for organizations integrating AI into their cybersecurity infrastructure. The workshop provided a forum for stakeholders to provide input to the Cyber AI Profile, including usability, scope, content, and alignment with existing cybersecurity and AI resources. By incorporating insights from participants across various organizations, the workshop established a collaborative foundation for addressing AI-specific cybersecurity challenges while enabling organizations to harness AI’s transformative potential.
contents.html_ja: 2026年1月14日、国立標準技術研究所（NIST）の国立サイバーセキュリティ卓越センター（NCCoE）は、2025年12月16日に公開された NIST Cybersecurity Framework Profile for Artificial Intelligence（Cyber AI Profile）[1] の予備ドラフトに関するフィードバックを集めるため、公開ワークショップ Cyber AI Profile Workshop #2 を開催しました。本書は、開会の挨拶、パネル、午前の発表、午後のブレイクアウトセッションを含む、ワークショップでの議論の概要を示します。このワークショップは、NIST における人工知能（AI）とサイバーセキュリティのプロジェクトへの認識を高め、AI をサイバーセキュリティ基盤に統合する組織にとっての優先分野についてフィードバックを得ることを目的としていました。ワークショップは、関係者が Cyber AI Profile に対して、使いやすさ、範囲、内容、既存のサイバーセキュリティおよび AI のリソースとの整合性などについて意見を寄せる場となりました。さまざまな組織の参加者の知見を取り入れることで、ワークショップは、AI 固有のサイバーセキュリティ課題に取り組むための協力的な基盤を築くとともに、組織が AI の変革的な可能性を活用できるようにしました。

contents.html: Recent advances in AI technologies bring great opportunities, but also new and modified cybersecurity risks and impacts that need to be managed. NIST is extending and adapting existing frameworks, such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (CSF 2.0) [2], to assist organizations as they face these new or expanded risks. The Cyber AI Profile is being developed in response to feedback from the cybersecurity and AI communities, indicating that there would be value in guidelines based on the CSF 2.0. The community was clear that there are opportunities for using AI to enhance cybersecurity capabilities, as well as new considerations for managing cybersecurity risk related to AI systems.
contents.html_ja: AI 技術の最近の進歩は大きな機会をもたらしますが、管理する必要のある、新しい、または変化したサイバーセキュリティのリスクと影響ももたらします。NIST は、組織がこれらの新しい、または拡大したリスクに直面する際に役立つよう、NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0（CSF 2.0）[2] などの既存のフレームワークを拡張し、適応させています。Cyber AI Profile は、CSF 2.0 に基づくガイドラインには価値があるというサイバーセキュリティおよび AI コミュニティからのフィードバックを受けて策定されています。コミュニティは、サイバーセキュリティ能力を強化するために AI を活用する機会があること、また AI システムに関連するサイバーセキュリティリスクを管理するための新たな検討事項があることを明確にしました。

contents.html: Organizations vary in how they use AI. Some organizations may not yet be using AI. Some may be using cybersecurity solutions enabled with machine learning (ML) technology for pattern detection and planning but have not yet adopted newer AI capabilities, such as Generative AI (genAI) or Agentic AI. Regardless of where organizations are on their AI journey, they need risk management approaches that support the realities of advancements in AI use to position them to defend against AI-enabled cyberattacks from adversaries and to leverage AI-enabled cyber defense capabilities. To address these emerging risks and opportunities, particularly in a rapidly evolving field, NIST is developing the Cyber AI Profile [1] to identify how organizations can leverage and adapt the CSF 2.0 [2] to manage AI-related cybersecurity risks effectively. The Cyber AI Profile will seek to help organizations integrate AI-specific considerations into existing cybersecurity programs by:
contents.html_ja: AI の使い方は組織によって異なります。まだ AI を使用していない組織もあるでしょう。パターン検出と計画のために機械学習（ML）技術を用いたサイバーセキュリティソリューションを使用しているものの、生成 AI（genAI）やエージェント型 AI などの新しい AI 能力はまだ採用していない組織もあるでしょう。組織が AI 活用のどの段階にあるかにかかわらず、AI を活用した攻撃者によるサイバー攻撃に対して防御し、AI を活用したサイバー防御能力を活用できるようにするために、AI 利用の進展という現実に対応したリスク管理のアプローチが必要です。特に急速に進化している分野で、これらの新たなリスクと機会に対処するため、NIST は、組織が AI 関連のサイバーセキュリティリスクを効果的に管理するために CSF 2.0 [2] をどのように活用し、適応させられるかを示す Cyber AI Profile [1] を策定しています。Cyber AI Profile は、次のことによって、組織が AI 固有の検討事項を既存のサイバーセキュリティプログラムに統合できるよう支援することを目指しています。

contents.html: The workshop provided a platform for exploring AI cybersecurity opportunities and challenges, and the potential role of the Cyber AI Profile in accelerating AI adoption by giving organizations confidence to address these challenges. Discussions during the workshop were intended to gather input from the community on securing AI components, leveraging AI for cyber defense, and thwarting AI-enabled attacks. Throughout the day, attendees engaged in dynamic conversations while speakers and panelists highlighted the importance of collaboration between the AI and cybersecurity communities to shape actionable implementation guidelines.
contents.html_ja: ワークショップは、AI のサイバーセキュリティに関する機会と課題、そして、これらの課題に対処する自信を組織に与えることで AI の導入を加速させる Cyber AI Profile の潜在的な役割を探る場となりました。ワークショップでの議論は、AI コンポーネントの保護、サイバー防御への AI の活用、AI を活用した攻撃の阻止について、コミュニティから意見を集めることを意図していました。1 日を通じて、参加者は活発な対話を行い、講演者とパネリストは、実行可能な実装ガイドラインを形づくるうえで、AI コミュニティとサイバーセキュリティコミュニティの協力が重要であることを強調しました。

contents.html: Participants in the workshop explored the cybersecurity opportunities and complex challenges introduced by AI systems, emphasizing the need for actionable solutions and cross-disciplinary collaboration to help organizations strategically adopt AI while addressing and prioritizing cybersecurity risks stemming from its advancements. Discussions included addressing risk management through a multidisciplinary approach enabled by strategic Focus Areas, as well as identifying challenges to AI-readiness and associated opportunities and risks, and forward-leaning approaches to address both. contents.html: Ms. Pascoe welcomed attendees and expressed appreciation for their engagement and collaboration. She reiterated that practical implementation guidance informed by community insights is essential to ensuring the Cyber AI Profile remains effective in addressing evolving AI capabilities and threats. She provided an overview of NIST’s and the NCCoE’s missions, which includes developing voluntary guidance on pressing cybersecurity challenges such as data protection, trusted enterprise, cybersecurity, and AI, as well as resilient embedded systems, through collaborative engagements with industry, government, and academia. Ms. Pascoe discussed how Cybersecurity Framework Community Profiles, such as the Cyber AI Profile, use the CSF to help organizations within a community understand common cybersecurity concerns and where to focus their efforts to prioritize and address cybersecurity opportunities and challenges. Ms. Pascoe noted that Profiles can also serve as a listening mechanism for NCCoE to understand shared opportunities, challenges, and concerns that reflect the community's expertise.

contents.html_ja: NIST サイバーセキュリティ・プライバシー・AI プログラムのプログラムマネージャー兼 Cyber AI Profile の共同リードである Katerina Megas 氏は、Cyber AI Profile の背景とロードマップ、ワークショップの目標と構成、そして、AI の幅広い導入が既存のサイバーセキュリティとプライバシーのリスクおよびリスク管理アプローチにどのような影響を及ぼしうるかの理解を含め、Profile が NIST のその他の AI プログラムや取り組みとどのように統合されるかを紹介しました。

contents.html: Ms. Megas shared the gaps heard from the cybersecurity community and how their insights shaped the Cyber AI Profile’s Focus Areas. The cybersecurity community wanted to understand opportunities to adopt AI, implications associated with those opportunities, and how AI is changing existing risk management measures. She observed that, in many organizations, leadership has made it a priority to understand how AI is being adopted and used, yet organizations are finding it challenging to think strategically about AI while balancing day-to-day responsibilities. The community also shared that the lack of a common taxonomy across AI publications and documentation is making it difficult for AI consumers and users to establish a consistent, clear understanding of how AI might impact them. Ms. Megas noted that the community expressed a desire to “not reinvent the wheel,” to build on existing frameworks and practices, identify gaps, and determine what is new or needs to be created to address those gaps.
contents.html_ja: Megas 氏は、サイバーセキュリティコミュニティから聞かれたギャップと、そこから得られた知見が Cyber AI Profile のフォーカスエリアをどのように形づくったかを紹介しました。サイバーセキュリティコミュニティは、AI を導入する機会、それらの機会に伴う影響、そして AI が既存のリスク管理策をどのように変えているかを理解したいと考えていました。同氏は、多くの組織で、経営層が AI がどのように導入され使われているかを理解することを優先事項としている一方で、組織は日常の責務とのバランスを取りながら AI について戦略的に考えることが難しいと感じていることを指摘しました。また、コミュニティからは、AI に関する刊行物や文書の間に共通の分類体系がないことが、AI の消費者や利用者が AI から受けうる影響について一貫した明確な理解を確立することを難しくしているという声も寄せられました。Megas 氏は、コミュニティが「車輪を再発明しない」こと、既存のフレームワークや実践を土台にすること、ギャップを特定すること、そしてそれらのギャップに対処するために何が新しいか、何を作る必要があるかを判断することを望んでいると述べました。

contents.html: Mr. Stanley stated that after releasing the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) [5] in 2023, the AI RMF team has maintained a long engagement with the community on what cybersecurity for AI systems means. Mr. Stanley emphasized that a key aspect included in the AI RMF is discussion on trustworthiness, and in the AI RMF, NIST is trying to understand and document how AI operates differently in a variety of familiar tasks. Mr. Stanley stated that NIST wants to understand how the community is using AI so that NIST can better identify the measures and approaches needed to establish trust in AI use. Mr. Stanley closed by stating that the AI RMF [5] looks at ways to establish consistency with the NIST Strategy for American Technology Leadership in the 21<sup>st</sup> Century, such that there is trust integrated into those technologies, practices, and AI uses [6].
contents.html_ja: Stanley 氏は、2023年に Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework（AI RMF 1.0）[5] を公開した後、AI RMF チームは、AI システムのサイバーセキュリティが何を意味するかについて、コミュニティと長く関わり続けてきたと述べました。Stanley 氏は、AI RMF に含まれる重要な側面の一つが信頼性に関する議論であり、AI RMF において NIST は、AI がさまざまなおなじみのタスクでどのように異なる動作をするかを理解し、文書化しようとしていることを強調しました。Stanley 氏は、NIST は、AI の利用における信頼を確立するために必要な対策とアプローチをより適切に特定できるよう、コミュニティがどのように AI を使用しているかを理解したいと考えていると述べました。Stanley 氏は、AI RMF [5] は NIST Strategy for American Technology Leadership in the 21<sup>st</sup> Century との整合性を確立する方法を検討しており、それによってこれらの技術、実践、AI の利用に信頼が組み込まれるようにする [6] と述べて締めくくりました。

contents.html: 2.2.2. Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) (Ms. Maia Hamin)
contents.html_ja: 2.2.2. Center for AI Standards and Innovation（CAISI）（Maia Hamin 氏）
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p13 を描画して照合。節 2.2.2 は第 3 階層なので、節番号の階層に合わせて見出しレベルを 4 にする。

contents.html: Ms. Hamin provided an overview of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) [7], which was reorganized and rechartered with a broader mission in early 2025. CAISI leads evaluations and assessments of United States (U.S.) and adversary AI systems, develops best practices and standards for improving AI security, and advances U.S. AI standards internationally. Ms. Hamin shared the activities completed to date to achieve these goals, highlighting work related to securing AI agents and agent systems and the security threats, risks, and challenges they face, which could hinder adoption and pose risks to public safety and national security. CAISI also develops voluntary practices to include automated benchmark evaluations of language models and AI agent systems [8]. Sharing such AI model evaluations on the state of model security, Ms. Hamin noted, can help consumers and decision-makers understand the relative security of these models. Ms. Hamin highlighted where CAISI continues to help improve the security of U.S. AI systems through the discovery of vulnerabilities and the development of guidelines and best practices. Ms. Hamin concluded by sharing how the community can get involved in CAISI, such as providing input on CAISI’s recently published “Request for Information Regarding Security Considerations for Artificial Intelligence Agents” [9].
contents.html_ja: Hamin 氏は、2025年初頭に、より広範な使命の下で再編・再設置された Center for AI Standards and Innovation（CAISI）[7] の概要を説明しました。CAISI は、米国および敵対国の AI システムの評価とアセスメントを主導し、AI セキュリティを改善するためのベストプラクティスと標準を策定し、米国の AI 標準を国際的に推進しています。Hamin 氏は、これらの目標を達成するためにこれまでに完了した活動を紹介し、特に、AI エージェントとエージェントシステムの保護、およびそれらが直面するセキュリティ上の脅威、リスク、課題に関する取り組みを取り上げました。これらは、導入を妨げ、公共の安全と国家安全保障にリスクをもたらす可能性があります。CAISI はまた、言語モデルと AI エージェントシステムの自動ベンチマーク評価を含む、自主的なプラクティスも策定しています [8]。Hamin 氏は、モデルのセキュリティの状態に関するこうした AI モデルの評価を共有することで、消費者や意思決定者がこれらのモデルの相対的なセキュリティを理解するのに役立つと述べました。Hamin 氏は、脆弱性の発見とガイドラインおよびベストプラクティスの策定を通じて、CAISI が米国の AI システムのセキュリティ改善に引き続き貢献している点を強調しました。Hamin 氏は、最近公開された CAISI の “Request for Information Regarding Security Considerations for Artificial Intelligence Agents” [9] への意見提出など、コミュニティが CAISI に関与できる方法を紹介して締めくくりました。

contents.html: 2.2.3. Adversarial Machine Learning (Dr. Apostol Vassilev, NIST)
contents.html_ja: 2.2.3. 敵対的機械学習（Apostol Vassilev 博士、NIST）
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p13 を描画して照合。節 2.2.3 は第 3 階層なので、節番号の階層に合わせて見出しレベルを 4 にする。

contents.html: Mr. Vassilev opened with an overview of areas considered part of adversarial AI, noting that trends have emerged that show a transition from static chatbots to agentic AI, which both give advice and take actions that can help automate workflows. Mr. Vassilev stated that while agentic AI can improve productivity, it simultaneously increases the attack surface available to attackers to exploit. Mr. Vassilev noted that over the last three to five years, there has been a recurring pattern where a large language model (LLM) is released and, within days of its release, reports emerge of successful attacks against that LLM. To understand why this pattern exists, Mr. Vassilev shared that NIST performed rigorous mathematical analysis on the robustness of guardrail mechanisms intended to thwart attacks on AI models. Results from this analysis led NIST to conclude that there are no guardrails universally robust enough to withstand adversarial attacks and the prompts available to jailbreak systems. Mr. Vassilev stated that to protect against such attacks, proactive adoption of adaptive defense strategies is necessary. These strategies should include continuous in-house red teaming and ongoing updates to guardrails, with the goal of discouraging adversaries by raising the threshold for the effort required to exploit LLMs. To support these strategic efforts, NIST plans to update the NIST 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations [10], to include agentic AI and the landscape of its attacks and potential mitigations to support the AI security community. Mr. Vassilev also noted the connection to the COSAiS project and this effort.
contents.html_ja: Vassilev 氏は、敵対的 AI の一部とみなされる分野の概要を説明して話を始め、静的なチャットボットから、助言を行い、ワークフローを自動化するのに役立つ行動も実行するエージェント型 AI への移行を示す傾向が現れていると指摘しました。Vassilev 氏は、エージェント型 AI は生産性を向上させうる一方で、攻撃者が悪用できる攻撃対象領域を同時に拡大させると述べました。Vassilev 氏は、過去 3 年から 5 年にわたり、大規模言語モデル（LLM）が公開され、その公開から数日以内に、その LLM に対する攻撃が成功したという報告が現れるというパターンが繰り返されてきたと指摘しました。このパターンが存在する理由を理解するため、NIST は、AI モデルへの攻撃を阻止することを目的としたガードレールの仕組みの堅牢性について、厳密な数学的分析を行ったと Vassilev 氏は説明しました。この分析の結果から NIST は、敵対的攻撃や、システムを脱獄するために利用できるプロンプトに耐えるのに十分なほど普遍的に堅牢なガードレールは存在しないと結論づけました。Vassilev 氏は、こうした攻撃から保護するには、適応型の防御戦略を積極的に採用する必要があると述べました。これらの戦略には、継続的な社内レッドチーミングとガードレールの継続的な更新が含まれるべきであり、LLM を悪用するために必要な労力の閾値を引き上げることで、攻撃者の意欲を削ぐことを目標とします。これらの戦略的な取り組みを支援するため、NIST は、NIST 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations [10] を更新し、エージェント型 AI と、その攻撃および潜在的な緩和策の状況を含めて AI セキュリティコミュニティを支援する予定です。Vassilev 氏は、COSAiS プロジェクトとこの取り組みとのつながりにも言及しました。

contents.html: 2.2.4. Dioptra (Mr. Harold Booth, NIST)
contents.html_ja: 2.2.4. Dioptra（Harold Booth 氏、NIST）
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p14 を描画して照合。節 2.2.4 は第 3 階層なので、節番号の階層に合わせて見出しレベルを 4 にする。

contents.html: Mr. Booth provided a description of Dioptra [11], noting that it serves as a test platform that allows evaluations of different AI systems in a reproducible manner and tracks their inputs and outputs, understanding the different models and scenarios as they relate to those inputs and outputs. Mr. Booth also gave an overview of the different use cases for Dioptra, enabling individuals, based on their areas of expertise, to obtain specific insights that can inform their work. Use cases mentioned by Mr. Booth included using Dioptra to conduct testing that supports the characterization and evaluation of an AI system prior to deployment as well as using Dioptra by researchers to understand how attacks and defenses might perform relative to a new model or training technique. Mr. Booth noted that Dioptra is available on GitHub as an open-source project, is in the process of being updated to version 1.1 (both the test platform and its associated documentation), and includes new features such as built-in support for artifact handling.
contents.html_ja: Booth 氏は Dioptra [11] について説明し、これはさまざまな AI システムの評価を再現可能な方法で行えるようにするテストプラットフォームであり、それらの入力と出力を追跡して、入力と出力に関連するさまざまなモデルとシナリオを理解できるようにするものだと述べました。Booth 氏はまた、Dioptra のさまざまなユースケースの概要も説明し、個人が専門分野に基づいて、自らの作業に役立つ具体的な知見を得られることを示しました。Booth 氏が挙げたユースケースには、展開前の AI システムの特性評価と評価を支援するテストの実施に Dioptra を使用すること、また、新しいモデルや学習手法に対して攻撃や防御がどのように機能しうるかを理解するために研究者が Dioptra を使用することが含まれました。Booth 氏は、Dioptra はオープンソースプロジェクトとして GitHub で公開されており、（テストプラットフォームと関連文書の両方について）バージョン 1.1 への更新作業が進行中で、成果物の取り扱いの組込みサポートなどの新機能が含まれると述べました。

contents.html: 2.2.5. Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) AI Profile (Mr. Harold Booth, NIST)
contents.html_ja: 2.2.5. Secure Software Development Framework（SSDF）AI Profile（Harold Booth 氏、NIST）
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p14 を描画して照合。節 2.2.5 は第 3 階層なので、節番号の階層に合わせて見出しレベルを 4 にする。

contents.html: Mr. Booth also gave an overview of the SSDF AI Profile (NIST SP 800-218A, Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile) [12]. Mr. Booth explained that the goal is to make the Profile broadly applicable to AI systems and to examine what is unique or new in AI system development. For example, system developers must also consider the larger scale of data used by AI systems, as well as the reliability and protection mechanisms against attacks, and data management activities such as cleaning and pre-processing. When developing AI systems, data and code must be tracked to understand what happens with data from the moment it is collected and how it is fed into training systems. Mr. Booth also noted that organizations need to be aware that reusing third-party AI models can introduce security concerns, such as providing threat vectors for adversaries to exploit NIST is assessing the timeline for updating the SSDF AI Profile published in July 2024. The SSDF [13], which serves as the basis for the SSDF AI Profile, was recently updated to version 1.2 (initial public draft [IPD]) [14], consistent with Executive Order 14306 [15]. The public comment period for the SSDF was from December 2025 to January 2026.
contents.html_ja: Booth 氏はまた、SSDF AI Profile（NIST SP 800-218A, Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile）[12] の概要も説明しました。Booth 氏は、目標は Profile を AI システムに広く適用できるものにすることと、AI システム開発で独特なもの、または新しいものを検討することだと説明しました。たとえば、システム開発者は、AI システムが使用するデータのより大きな規模、攻撃に対する信頼性と保護の仕組み、クリーニングや前処理などのデータ管理活動も考慮しなければなりません。AI システムを開発するときには、データが収集された時点から何が起こり、どのように学習システムに投入されるかを理解するために、データとコードを追跡しなければなりません。Booth 氏はまた、サードパーティの AI モデルを再利用すると、攻撃者が悪用できる脅威ベクトルをもたらすなど、セキュリティ上の懸念が生じうることを、組織は認識する必要があると指摘しました。NIST は、2024年7月に公開された SSDF AI Profile を更新する時期を評価しています。SSDF AI Profile の基礎となる SSDF [13] は、大統領令 14306 [15] に沿って、最近バージョン 1.2（初期公開ドラフト [IPD]）[14] に更新されました。SSDF のパブリックコメント期間は、2025年12月から2026年1月まででした。

contents.html: 2.2.6. Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PETs) Testbed (Dr. Gary Howarth, NIST)
contents.html_ja: 2.2.6. Privacy Enhancing Technologies（PETs）Testbed（Gary Howarth 博士、NIST）
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p15 を描画して照合。節 2.2.6 は第 3 階層なので、節番号の階層に合わせて見出しレベルを 4 にする。

contents.html: The PETs program conducts investigations into privacy-enhancing technologies, which are technical tools or controls intended to reduce privacy risks arising from the collection, sharing, and processing of potentially sensitive data. Mr. Howarth described the PETs program [16] as producing guidelines and frameworks to evaluate and manage privacy risks. Mr. Howarth shared that NIST is developing the PETs testbed at the NCCoE, which will include benchmark data and model test deployments to demonstrate how PETs are deployed and investigate trade-offs, with the goal of creating a comprehensive set of tools to guide organizations when selecting and deploying PETs and managing privacy risks. Mr. Howarth continued by stating that PETs programs, to include the NIST Collaborative Research Cycle (CRC) [17], are complementary to AI risk management efforts. The CRC program is the largest collection of synthetic data for benchmarking exercises related to privacy. Under the CRC program, NIST is analyzing the consequences of using and training AI/ML with synthetic data and is exploring the impacts on AI/ML performance.
contents.html_ja: PETs プログラムは、プライバシー強化技術について調査を行っています。これは、機微な可能性のあるデータの収集、共有、処理から生じるプライバシーリスクを低減することを意図した技術的なツールまたは管理策です。Howarth 氏は、PETs プログラム [16] は、プライバシーリスクを評価し管理するためのガイドラインとフレームワークを作成していると説明しました。Howarth 氏は、NIST が NCCoE で PETs テストベッドを開発しており、これにはベンチマークデータとモデルのテスト展開が含まれ、PETs がどのように展開されるかを示し、トレードオフを調査して、PETs の選択と展開、およびプライバシーリスクの管理において組織を導く包括的なツール群を作ることを目標としていると述べました。Howarth 氏は続けて、NIST Collaborative Research Cycle（CRC）[17] を含む PETs プログラムは、AI リスク管理の取り組みを補完するものだと述べました。CRC プログラムは、プライバシーに関連するベンチマーク演習のための合成データの最大の集合です。CRC プログラムの下で、NIST は、合成データを使用して AI/ML を学習させ、使用した場合の影響を分析しており、AI/ML の性能への影響を調べています。

contents.html: Mr. Howarth spoke about a second program that is demonstrating how to apply privacy-preserving federated learning (PPFL). Federated learning connects ML among unconnected devices, enabling increases to both compute power and the amount of data available to train ML algorithms. PPFL introduces important privacy considerations, which NIST’s privacy-preserving federated learning platform is being used to investigate. NIST is asking questions about how different privatization mechanisms affect ML performance and which security and privacy controls are needed. NIST plans to publish model code as well as a complementary privacy and cybersecurity threat modeling example that shows the types of threats that PPFL is attempting to manage and applicable privacy and cybersecurity controls. Mr. Howarth concluded by noting that reducing privacy threats requires a strong cybersecurity foundation and emphasized that using synthetic data alone does not adequately protect privacy unless the original data is also secured.
contents.html_ja: Howarth 氏は、プライバシー保護連合学習（PPFL）の適用方法を実証している 2 つ目のプログラムについても話しました。連合学習は、つながっていないデバイス間で ML を結び付け、計算能力と、ML アルゴリズムの学習に利用できるデータ量の両方を増やせるようにします。PPFL は重要なプライバシー上の考慮事項をもたらし、NIST のプライバシー保護連合学習プラットフォームがその調査に使われています。NIST は、さまざまな秘匿化メカニズムが ML の性能にどのように影響するか、どのようなセキュリティ管理策とプライバシー管理策が必要かについて問いを立てています。NIST は、モデルコードに加えて、PPFL が管理しようとしている脅威の種類と、適用可能なプライバシー管理策およびサイバーセキュリティ管理策を示す、プライバシーとサイバーセキュリティの脅威モデリングの補完的な例を公開する予定です。Howarth 氏は、プライバシーの脅威を低減するには強固なサイバーセキュリティ基盤が必要であると述べ、元のデータも保護されていない限り、合成データを使用するだけではプライバシーを十分に保護できないことを強調して締めくくりました。

contents.html: 2.2.7. Agent Identities (Mr. Ryan Galluzzo, NIST)
contents.html_ja: 2.2.7. エージェントのアイデンティティ（Ryan Galluzzo 氏、NIST）
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p15 を描画して照合。節 2.2.7 は第 3 階層なので、節番号の階層に合わせて見出しレベルを 4 にする。

contents.html: Mr. Galluzzo opened by acknowledging that AI agents are starting to change the context and conversation around traditional cybersecurity controls, including regarding issues on agent access and identifying agents operating in organizations, how to authenticate an agent and verify it is what it claims to be, and how to authorize and manage access on an ongoing basis for agents to engage with data or take particular action, such as accessing data or resources, and necessary restrictions on those actions to address concerns that may result from data aggregation.
contents.html_ja: Galluzzo 氏は、AI エージェントが、従来のサイバーセキュリティ管理策をめぐる状況と議論を変え始めていることを認めて話を始めました。これには、エージェントのアクセスや、組織内で動作するエージェントの識別に関する問題、エージェントを認証し、それが主張どおりのものであることを検証する方法、エージェントがデータとやり取りしたり、データやリソースへのアクセスなどの特定の行動をとったりするためのアクセスを継続的に認可し管理する方法、そしてデータ集約から生じうる懸念に対処するためのそれらの行動への必要な制限が含まれます。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p15 を描画して照合。文言・種別とも原本どおり。

contents.html: NIST is examining the current state of the identity management space and the tools applied today to individual users and to certain software—or machine-to-machine-based systems—and how that context is changing with systems that can ingest external or internal data sources, analyze them, and potentially take actions [18][19]. Mr. Galluzzo explained that this analysis helps NIST understand the areas of change and impact to existing standards and any solutions, including determining if existing standards can be applied or updated, if new guidance (e.g., Profiles) may be needed to address gaps and new context, how to build in a reference architecture that will inform configuration, or recommended best practices.
contents.html_ja: NIST は、アイデンティティ管理分野の現状と、現在個々のユーザーや特定のソフトウェア（またはマシン間ベースのシステム）に適用されているツール、そして、外部または内部のデータソースを取り込み、分析し、行動をとる可能性のあるシステムによって、その状況がどのように変わりつつあるかを調べています [18][19]。Galluzzo 氏は、この分析は、変化の領域と、既存の標準およびあらゆる解決策への影響を NIST が理解するのに役立つと説明しました。これには、既存の標準を適用または更新できるか、ギャップと新たな状況に対処するために新しいガイダンス（たとえば Profile）が必要となるか、構成や推奨されるベストプラクティスの指針となるリファレンスアーキテクチャをどのように組み込むかの判断が含まれます。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p15〜p16 を描画して照合。「if new guidance (e.g., / Profiles) may be needed …」はページをまたぐ 1 段落。

contents.html: The Agent Identities work focuses on understanding and creating authorization flows and delegations pertaining to created agents, specifically determining the individual(s) who will be accountable for actions the AI system may take and how to bind the identity of that individual to the actions the agent is taking so organizations can audit, log, and understand the chains of trust related to agent actions. This work also considers human-in-the-loop scenarios, such as specifying who is notified and who decides whether to grant access when an agent tries to access data it is not authorized to use. Mr. Galluzzo concluded by noting that it is important to understand the balance between the benefits of agents operating within an enterprise and the need to protect the information an agent might access to preserve privacy, security, and confidentiality, to help inform where adaptations may be needed.
contents.html_ja: エージェントのアイデンティティに関する取り組みは、作成されたエージェントに関する認可フローと委任を理解し、作成することに重点を置いています。具体的には、AI システムがとりうる行動に責任を負う個人を特定すること、および、組織がエージェントの行動に関する信頼の連鎖を監査し、記録し、理解できるよう、その個人のアイデンティティをエージェントがとっている行動に結び付ける方法を特定することです。この取り組みでは、エージェントが使用を許可されていないデータにアクセスしようとしたときに、誰に通知し、誰がアクセスを許可するかを決めるなど、ヒューマン・イン・ザ・ループのシナリオも検討します。Galluzzo 氏は、どこで適応が必要になるかを判断する材料とするために、企業内でエージェントが動作することの利点と、プライバシー、セキュリティ、機密性を維持するためにエージェントがアクセスしうる情報を保護する必要性とのバランスを理解することが重要であると述べて締めくくりました。

contents.html: Mr. Lee opened with an overview of the NCCoE Chatbot [20], stating that the Chatbot was designed to increase the efficiency and ease of conducting searches on the wealth of information the NCCoE has available on its website. The NCCoE Chatbot uses a customized retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based LLM to assist with searching large amounts of data. The customized RAG-LLM includes a metadata layer designed to “filter down” the search index, focusing on specific keywords or information before the Chatbot conducts a semantic similarity vector comparison to produce its search results. Mr. Lee noted that including the metadata layer in the Chatbot is intended to address the lag in responses that occurs as the search index grows.
contents.html_ja: Lee 氏は NCCoE チャットボット [20] の概要を説明して話を始め、このチャットボットは、NCCoE がウェブサイトで提供している豊富な情報の検索の効率と容易さを高めるために設計されたと述べました。NCCoE チャットボットは、大量のデータの検索を支援するために、カスタマイズされた検索拡張生成（RAG）ベースの LLM を使用しています。カスタマイズされた RAG-LLM には、チャットボットが意味的類似性のベクトル比較を行って検索結果を生成する前に、特定のキーワードや情報に焦点を当てて検索インデックスを「絞り込む」ように設計されたメタデータ層が含まれています。Lee 氏は、チャットボットにメタデータ層を含めるのは、検索インデックスが大きくなるにつれて生じる応答の遅延に対処するためであると述べました。

contents.html: Moving to the discussion on the Emerging Technology Accelerators, Dr. Schlenoff mentioned the December 2025 establishment of the “AI Accelerator,” [22] which will include the “AI Economic Security Center for U.S. Manufacturing Productivity” and the “AI Economic Security Center to Secure U.S. Critical Infrastructure from Cyberthreats.” Dr. Schlenoff provided overviews of each of these areas in the AI Accelerator. Dr. Schlenoff acknowledged that these areas remain broad and NIST remains consistently active in collaboration and outreach with the community to understand key challenges where impact can be made, highlighting that collaborations with industry, academia, and others are leveraged to inform conversations that identify core challenges that can be solved and work closely with those stakeholders to do so. Dr. Schlenoff noted that there are opportunities to involve academia, whether during pre-standardization development (e.g., participation in research that will inform the standards) or during standard development (e.g., through standards bodies). NIST is working with academic partners but is open to exploring increased engagement and involvement.

contents.html: Dr. Schlenoff explained that NIST’s strategy is to create “unprecedented AI ‘gold standards’”. contents.html: Ms. Snyder then spoke specifically about the Cyber AI Profile and how collaborative discussions informed its development. The Profile is designed to be broadly applicable, so organizations can implement it in ways that support many different AI adoption and use scenarios and a variety of roles, including developing AI systems, using AI technologies, capitalizing on cybersecurity capabilities AI can provide, and seeking to better understand and defend against adversarial use of AI to conduct attacks. This approach focuses the Profile on cybersecurity and AI-specific opportunities and concerns when designing or deploying an AI system, rather than on providing engineering guidance.

contents.html: The Secure Focus Area breakouts spent significant time on governance-related topics, particularly accountability, ownership, and risk management. One of the key challenges and concerns stressed by participants across all Track A sessions was that AI governance moves more slowly than AI innovation. Additionally, practitioners are struggling to identify and explain AI and AI risk, including finding where AI lives in their environments. Accountability, in particular, garnered attention with subtopics including AI visibility within organizations, understanding responsibilities for specific roles (e.g., developer, deployer, user), the increasing complexity of human oversight as agentic AI capabilities expand, and concerns over the relationship between accountability and liability. The lack of clarity in these areas makes it difficult to identify and manage AI risks.

contents.html: 2.5.1. Presentation: Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems (COSAiS) (Ms. Victoria Pillitteri, NIST)
contents.html_ja: 2.5.1. 発表: Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems（COSAiS）（Victoria Pillitteri 氏、NIST）

contents.html: Ms. Pillitteri opened by sharing the drivers for the COSAiS project, describing the feedback from the community to develop technical implementation guidance for securing AI systems leveraging existing standards and guidelines to the maximum extent, complementing the Cyber AI Profile. She provided an overview of the NIST SP 800-53 controls catalog [23], emphasizing that any organization can leverage the broad collection of cybersecurity and privacy outcomes to determine which controls work for them to manage risk and should not be implemented in totality. Ms. Pillitteri stated that because the controls needed to manage cybersecurity and privacy risks to AI systems are largely similar to what would be needed for any type of software, the community can leverage the existing NIST SP 800-53 control catalog as a starting point. She acknowledged that since the controls are not specific to any given technology or AI systems, the COSAiS work seeks to identify subsets of controls especially relevant for AI systems to better help developers and implementers.
contents.html_ja: Pillitteri 氏は、COSAiS プロジェクトの推進要因を紹介して話を始めました。コミュニティから寄せられた、Cyber AI Profile を補完し、既存の標準とガイドラインを最大限に活用して AI システムを保護するための技術的な実装ガイダンスを策定してほしいという要望について説明しました。同氏は、NIST SP 800-53 管理策カタログ [23] の概要を説明し、あらゆる組織が、サイバーセキュリティとプライバシーの成果の幅広い集合を活用して、リスク管理にどの管理策が適しているかを判断でき、カタログの管理策をすべて一律に実装する必要はないと強調しました。Pillitteri 氏は、AI システムのサイバーセキュリティリスクとプライバシーリスクの管理に必要な管理策は、あらゆる種類のソフトウェアに必要なものと大部分が似ているため、コミュニティは既存の NIST SP 800-53 管理策カタログを出発点として活用できると述べました。同氏は、管理策が特定の技術や AI システムに固有のものではないことを認めたうえで、COSAiS の取り組みは、開発者と実装者をより適切に支援するために、AI システムに特に関連する管理策のサブセットを特定しようとしていると説明しました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p23 を描画して照合。文言・種別とも原本どおり。

contents.html: Ms. Pillitteri explained that control overlays can be either a fully specified set of controls that is inclusive of a baseline or a small subset of controls tailored to address a specific community or organization need, such as an environment of operation or type of system. Within these control overlays, the overlay can provide further details, such as defining specific parameter values and setting potential frequency values.
contents.html_ja: Pillitteri 氏は、コントロールオーバーレイには、ベースラインを含む完全に規定された管理策の集合の場合と、運用環境やシステムの種類など、特定のコミュニティや組織のニーズに対応するように調整された管理策の小さなサブセットの場合があると説明しました。これらのコントロールオーバーレイの中で、オーバーレイは、特定のパラメータ値の定義や、設定可能な頻度値の設定など、さらに詳細な内容を提供できます。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p23 を描画して照合。文言・種別とも原本どおり。

contents.html: Ms. Pillitteri shared that COSAiS provides an opportunity to work with the community to complement the Profile and provide implementation-specific guidance for different types of AI systems (e.g., predictive AI, genAI, single- and multi-agent AI, and controls for security developers). Within the COSAiS project, these existing controls will be tailored to manage risk specific to types and uses of AI systems. By developing multiple overlays, each will focus on managing the different cybersecurity and privacy risks associated with different types of AI systems, and each overlay will have a target audience and focus. The goal is for the overlays to work alone or in combination, allowing organizations the flexibility to determine which overlay(s) to apply based on their unique needs. The COSAiS can also leverage the assessment guidance that exists for the control catalog and other risk management guidance.
contents.html_ja: Pillitteri 氏は、COSAiS は、コミュニティと協力して Profile を補完し、さまざまな種類の AI システム（たとえば、予測 AI、生成 AI、単一エージェントおよびマルチエージェント AI、セキュリティ開発者向けの管理策）に対する実装固有のガイダンスを提供する機会であると述べました。COSAiS プロジェクトでは、これらの既存の管理策が、AI システムの種類と用途に固有のリスクを管理するように調整されます。複数のオーバーレイを策定することで、それぞれが異なる種類の AI システムに関連する異なるサイバーセキュリティリスクとプライバシーリスクの管理に焦点を当て、各オーバーレイには想定読者と焦点が定められます。目標は、オーバーレイを単独でも組み合わせても使えるようにし、組織が自らの固有のニーズに基づいて、どのオーバーレイを適用するかを柔軟に決定できるようにすることです。COSAiS は、管理策カタログに存在する評価ガイダンスやその他のリスク管理ガイダンスも活用できます。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p23 を描画して照合。文言・種別とも原本どおり。

contents.html: Ms. Pillitteri reviewed the proposed methodology in the “NIST SP 800-53 Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems Concept Paper” [24] issued during the summer of 2025 and built upon by the recently released “NIST SP 800-53 Control Overlay for Securing AI Systems: Using and Fine Tuning Predictive AI (Annotated Outline for Cyber AI Profile Workshop #2)” [25]. She discussed the contents of the annotated outline for the initial “Using and Fine-Tuning Predictive AI” overlay, emphasizing that the final decisions regarding the overlay are pending stakeholder feedback and insights.
contents.html_ja: Pillitteri 氏は、2025年夏に発行された “NIST SP 800-53 Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems Concept Paper” [24] で提案された方法論と、それを土台として最近公開された “NIST SP 800-53 Control Overlay for Securing AI Systems: Using and Fine Tuning Predictive AI (Annotated Outline for Cyber AI Profile Workshop #2)” [25] を確認しました。同氏は、最初の “Using and Fine-Tuning Predictive AI” オーバーレイの注釈付きアウトラインの内容について論じ、オーバーレイに関する最終決定は関係者のフィードバックと知見を待っていると強調しました。

contents.html: Ms. Pillitteri emphasized that understanding the gaps between controls that organizations may currently implement, and the additional controls needed to secure AI systems, is critical to creating control overlays that are “lightweight but impactful.” To develop resources to meet stakeholder needs, NIST consistently engages in outreach and collaboration with stakeholders, such as through workshops and Slack community discussions.<sup>4</sup> One area of feedback NIST is seeking is whether the overlays should be based on the NIST SP 800-53B [26] Moderate baseline. The COSAiS is based on several assumptions, such as an existing cybersecurity risk management program.
contents.html_ja: Pillitteri 氏は、組織が現在実装している可能性のある管理策と、AI システムを保護するために必要な追加の管理策との間のギャップを理解することが、「軽量だが影響力のある」コントロールオーバーレイを作成するうえで重要であると強調しました。関係者のニーズを満たすリソースを策定するため、NIST は、ワークショップや Slack のコミュニティでの議論などを通じて、関係者とのアウトリーチと協力に一貫して取り組んでいます。<sup>4</sup> NIST が求めているフィードバックの一つは、オーバーレイを NIST SP 800-53B [26] の Moderate ベースラインに基づかせるべきかどうかです。COSAiS は、既存のサイバーセキュリティリスク管理プログラムの存在など、いくつかの前提に基づいています。

contents.html: Participant discussions during the COSAiS sessions emphasized the importance of NIST making the case for why the COSAiS are needed, using clear, direct language to support the overlays. Discussions also highlighted the need to focus the overlays’ guidance on small businesses, which are typically more constrained or have less access to resources to support cybersecurity initiatives and activities, and noted that the controls identified should not be too strict or inhibit innovation. Participants suggested that NIST consider using the Low-impact baseline rather than the currently proposed Moderate baseline.

contents.html: The Cyber AI Profile Workshop offered participants an opportunity to share with NIST feedback and insights throughout the day on the draft Cyber AI Profile. The themes summarized below reflect perspectives raised by workshop participants and are intended to inform NIST’s continued development of the Cyber AI Profile and other NIST programs. Overall, participants expressed support for the development of the Cyber AI Profile and appreciated that it is filling gaps in guidance. They emphasized the need for both enterprise risk management [27][28][29] and implementation-level resources, especially to benefit smaller organizations or organizations overwhelmed with addressing strategic adoption, integration, and use of AI while continuing to manage an already full load of ongoing tactical and operational cybersecurity risk management activities. The following takeaways are the ideas, observations, and suggestions that NIST heard from workshop participants and received significant support from them. This workshop was not a forum for developing consensus; rather, the takeaways represent recurrent themes that emerged during discussions and not formal positions taken by participants. This document cannot capture every thought, opinion, and suggestion provided during the workshop. These takeaways do not represent NIST recommendations or guidelines; rather, they provide important feedback to the program and serve as a basis for future conversations with the community and NIST’s continued development of the Cyber AI Profile as a practical resource for organizations navigating AI-related opportunities and risks.
contents.html_ja: Cyber AI Profile ワークショップは、参加者が 1 日を通じて、Cyber AI Profile のドラフトに関するフィードバックと知見を NIST と共有する機会となりました。以下にまとめたテーマは、ワークショップの参加者が提起した見解を反映しており、NIST による Cyber AI Profile およびその他の NIST プログラムの継続的な策定に役立てることを意図しています。全体として、参加者は Cyber AI Profile の策定を支持し、それがガイダンスのギャップを埋めていることを評価しました。参加者は、特に、AI の戦略的な導入、統合、利用に取り組みながら、すでに多忙な日常の戦術的・運用的なサイバーセキュリティリスク管理活動も続けなければならない小規模な組織や、対応に追われる組織のために、エンタープライズリスク管理 [27][28][29] と実装レベルのリソースの両方が必要であることを強調しました。以下の収穫は、NIST がワークショップの参加者から聞いた、参加者から大きな支持を得た考え、所見、提案です。このワークショップは合意形成の場ではありませんでした。収穫は、議論の中で繰り返し現れたテーマを表すものであり、参加者がとった公式の立場ではありません。本書は、ワークショップで寄せられたすべての考え、意見、提案を網羅できるものではありません。これらの収穫は、NIST の推奨事項やガイドラインを表すものではなく、プログラムに対する重要なフィードバックを提供し、コミュニティとの今後の対話と、AI 関連の機会とリスクに取り組む組織にとって実用的なリソースとなるよう NIST が Cyber AI Profile の策定を続けるうえでの基礎となるものです。

contents.html: From an integrity perspective, a lack of visibility into the data used to train AI models, or into the models themselves, is a concern. This includes a lack of visibility into how AI models are trained in products and services from suppliers and third-party vendors. Participants stated that organizations need to know what data was used in a model so they can explain AI actions and functions to end users to increase the trustworthiness of AI. This includes organizational ability to communicate clearly to leadership to establish trustworthiness related to the use of AI and AI-driven decisions (whether made by AI or users informed by AI).
contents.html_ja: 完全性の観点から、AI モデルの学習に使われたデータやモデル自体が可視化されていないことは懸念事項です。これには、サプライヤーやサードパーティベンダーの製品やサービスで AI モデルがどのように学習されているかが可視化されていないことが含まれます。参加者は、AI の信頼性を高めるために、AI の行動と機能をエンドユーザーに説明できるよう、組織はモデルにどのようなデータが使われたかを知る必要があると述べました。これには、AI の利用と AI による意思決定（AI が行う場合も、AI の支援を受けた利用者が行う場合も）に関する信頼性を確立するために、経営層に明確に伝える組織の能力が含まれます。

contents.html: Throughout the workshop, participants highlighted several important themes that extend beyond the immediate scope of the Cyber AI Profile. While these topics will not be directly addressed through the Profile, they represent valuable insights regarding community needs:

contents.html: Scalable and Adaptable Tools: The need for scalable and adaptable tools to manage AI-related cybersecurity risks was emphasized. Participants suggested interactive and customizable design features for the Cyber AI Profile, such as NIST Online Informative References (OLIR) [30]-based mappings and LLM integration, to make the Profile more user-friendly and applicable across diverse industries. These discussions extended beyond the level of sophistication suggested by earlier comments regarding simpler sorting capabilities to include the ability to sort COSAiS content by lifecycle stage.
contents.html_ja: スケーラブルで適応可能なツール: AI 関連のサイバーセキュリティリスクを管理するための、スケーラブルで適応可能なツールの必要性が強調されました。参加者は、Profile をよりユーザーフレンドリーにし、多様な業界に適用できるようにするために、NIST Online Informative References（OLIR）[30] ベースの対応付けや LLM との統合など、Cyber AI Profile のインタラクティブでカスタマイズ可能な設計機能を提案しました。これらの議論は、より単純な並べ替え機能に関する以前のコメントで示されたものより高度な内容にまで及び、COSAiS の内容をライフサイクルの段階で並べ替える機能も含んでいました。

contents.html: Workforce Development and Guidance: Participants emphasized the need for workforce training to address AI-related cybersecurity challenges, including adopting AI for cybersecurity. Challenges with the speed and velocity of AI adoption and AI attacks emphasize the importance of workforce training and awareness to recognize and defend against adversarial AI attacks. Workforce-related guidance may include decisions to align workforce roles and resources with AI capabilities and applications.
contents.html_ja: 人材の育成とガイダンス: 参加者は、サイバーセキュリティのための AI の導入を含め、AI 関連のサイバーセキュリティ課題に対処するための人材育成が必要であることを強調しました。AI の急速な導入と AI 攻撃は、敵対的な AI 攻撃を認識して防御するための人材育成と意識向上の重要性を浮き彫りにしています。人材に関するガイダンスには、人材の役割とリソースを AI の能力と応用に整合させる判断が含まれる場合があります。

contents.html: Procurement Process Guidance: Practitioners need consistent guidance in the procurement process for new technologies (e.g., libraries, models, data) to support risk management decision-making related to AI. Addressing gaps in guidance enables more informed risk management decision-making by clarifying how to determine and communicate risk associated with new AI systems, identify the assurances that need to be in place, and use existing application and data risk assessment sources to adequately answer the risk questions raised by these new technologies.
contents.html_ja: 調達プロセスのガイダンス: 実務担当者には、AI に関連するリスク管理の意思決定を支援するために、新しい技術（たとえば、ライブラリ、モデル、データ）の調達プロセスにおける一貫したガイダンスが必要です。ガイダンスのギャップに対処することで、新しい AI システムに関連するリスクを判断し伝える方法、整備する必要のある保証を特定する方法、そしてこれらの新しい技術によって生じるリスクの問いに十分に答えるために既存のアプリケーションとデータのリスクアセスメントの情報源を使う方法が明確になり、より情報に基づいたリスク管理の意思決定が可能になります。

contents.html: NIST continues to follow the Cyber AI Profile Roadmap which can be found on the NCCoE Cyber AI Profile project page. This roadmap is a living document that reflects the overall steps NIST will complete to create the Cyber AI Profile. Each step of the process toward the Final Cyber AI Profile builds on prior actions and information, including workshops and public comment periods. The Cyber AI Profile preliminary draft and Workshop #2 were informed by research conducted by the team and stakeholder comments received during previous activities in the roadmap. NIST will leverage the information collected from Workshop #2 as well as the comments submitted on the Cyber AI Profile preliminary draft, and future research and engagement activities to guide the next version of the Cyber AI Profile (the IPD) for public comment in summer 2026.
contents.html_ja: NIST は、NCCoE の Cyber AI Profile プロジェクトのページにある Cyber AI Profile Roadmap に引き続き従っています。このロードマップは、NIST が Cyber AI Profile を作成するために完了する全体的なステップを反映した、継続的に更新される文書です。最終版の Cyber AI Profile に向けたプロセスの各ステップは、ワークショップやパブリックコメント期間を含む、それ以前の行動と情報の上に積み上げられます。Cyber AI Profile の予備ドラフトとワークショップ #2 には、チームが行った調査と、ロードマップのそれ以前の活動で受け取った関係者のコメントが反映されました。NIST は、ワークショップ #2 から集めた情報、Cyber AI Profile の予備ドラフトに寄せられたコメント、今後の調査および関係者とのエンゲージメント活動を活用して、2026年夏にパブリックコメントに付す Cyber AI Profile の次のバージョン（IPD）の策定を導きます。

Mr. Stanley stated that after releasing the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) [5] in 2023, the AI RMF team has maintained a long engagement with the community on what cybersecurity for AI systems means. Mr. Stanley emphasized that a key aspect included in the AI RMF is discussion on trustworthiness, and in the AI RMF, NIST is trying to understand and document how AI operates differently in a variety of familiar tasks. Mr. Stanley stated that NIST wants to understand how the community is using AI so that NIST can better identify the measures and approaches needed to establish trust in AI use. Mr. Stanley closed by stating that the AI RMF [5] looks at ways to establish consistency with the NIST Strategy for American Technology Leadership in the 21st Century, such that there is trust integrated into those technologies, practices, and AI uses [6].

Dr. Schlenoff opened with an overview of the Administration’s science and technology priorities and how those priorities are shaping emerging research on technologies such as AI and quantum information technology (QIT). NIST, guided by the Administration’s priorities, developed the NIST Strategy for American Technology Leadership in the 21st Century, which includes AI considerations across its four areas. Dr. Schlenoff focused the discussion on specific areas related to American AI innovation and the acceleration of manufacturing productivity; protecting and securing U.S. critical infrastructure; measuring AI system performance, reliability, and security; and rapidly evaluating AI system capabilities to promote AI innovation, which aligns with work under CAISI.

Ms. Pillitteri emphasized that understanding the gaps between controls that organizations may currently implement, and the additional controls needed to secure AI systems, is critical to creating control overlays that are “lightweight but impactful.” To develop resources to meet stakeholder needs, NIST consistently engages in outreach and collaboration with stakeholders, such as through workshops and Slack community discussions.4 One area of feedback NIST is seeking is whether the overlays should be based on the NIST SP 800-53B [26] Moderate baseline. The COSAiS is based on several assumptions, such as an existing cybersecurity risk management program.

Participants also suggested that developing guidance and/or methods for prioritization based on maturity and risk could be valuable (e.g., with greater nuance than currently provided, perhaps based on use cases, risk factors, or methods).

NIST continues to follow the Cyber AI Profile Roadmap which can be found on the NCCoE Cyber AI Profile project page. This roadmap is a living document that reflects the overall steps NIST will complete to create the Cyber AI Profile. Each step of the process toward the Final Cyber AI

Profile builds on prior actions and information, including workshops and public comment periods. The Cyber AI Profile preliminary draft and Workshop #2 were informed by research conducted by the team and stakeholder comments received during previous activities in the roadmap. NIST will leverage the information collected from Workshop #2 as well as the comments submitted on the Cyber AI Profile preliminary draft, and future research and engagement activities to guide the next version of the Cyber AI Profile (the IPD) for public comment in summer 2026.

Participants indicated that responsibility for AI-driven decisions typically falls on o those lines of business deploying the AI but noted that responsibility may shift among different lines of business.
Participants also cautioned that the term “accountability” could be interpreted o as “liability.”

Participants noted it can be difficult to determine where AI systems, including o “shadow AI,” are in an enterprise and what components outside the enterprise the AI might need to access. Understanding these AI deployments is a precursor to securing the AI system.

Regarding vendors and vendor-provided technologies, participants stressed o difficulties in managing AI risk in vendor technologies, with some vendors being more helpful in mitigating risk than others. Participants also mentioned it is not possible to clearly understand which vendors are securing or developing AI “properly,” and this knowledge gap further complicates the procurement process.

Another area participants stressed was how to fail gracefully and revert to o normal operations when AI systems do not operate as intended (i.e., cyber resiliency for operating AI, rollback of AI systems).
Respond (e.g., remediating vulnerabilities; decreasing mean time in responding o to AI attacks; enhancing communications and the cadence of response activities following an incident).

Recover (e.g., generating After Action Reports [AARs] to create a succinct o narrative of an event, including timestamps; analysis of what went wrong; recommendations regarding prioritized mitigation strategies).
Explore how to determine responsibility in AI and AI agent actions in chains of o custody that reflect development, training, implementation, and use by different parties.

Risk management becomes increasingly important, including determining and o communicating what risks are acceptable and at what levels. Dynamic tools or mechanisms to maintain communications about how adversaries are using AI to conduct attacks and how those attacks are being identified and mitigated may help, such as a repository of prompt injection attacks.
Subcategories in the CSF Respond Function can help address this cybersecurity o need, including communications on risk responses and risk management needs.
Participants expressed the value of establishing the context of a baseline in the o overlays and whether the baseline serves as a starting point or is intended to represent the final control set.

Participants shared that it would be helpful to implementers and users of the o COSAiS for NIST to consider shifting from a baseline to a modular approach for greater tailoring and adaptation by different organizations and industries with varying backgrounds, needs, environments, and AI use.
A request was made for additional information on the decision to develop o COSAiS using existing controls rather than have NIST develop new controls specific to AI.

General information to include: the relationship between the Cyber AI Profile o and the CSF (e.g., visual depiction of the relationship versus text); content that conveys to users the “why” to support planning and implementation of capability development; the general need for the Cyber AI Profile as AI is widespread and rapidly becoming ubiquitous within organizations; and how to use in combination the Cyber AI Profile, the CSF 2.0, and the AI RMF when building a single, operational view of risk.

The Profile was perceived by participants as deployment-focused. Participants o asked NIST to expand the content to include how to improve the cybersecurity of AI systems during development in anticipation of how the AI will be deployed and used.
Clarification of the definitions for the three Focus Area terms and potentially o additional visuals that help distinguish the Focus Areas’ scopes.
Formats that support sortable views, such as viewing only the Priority 1 or o dropdown boxes that enable analysis of different levels of detail for the Subcategories.

The inclusion of additional guidance on topics such as addressing insider threats o posed by both humans and AI; prioritization assistance (e.g., through use of a consequence tiering model); and AI nuances that are inherent in Priority 3 Subcategories that may not yet exist in organizations.
Include hyperlinks to AI resources and other guidance where possible, such as in o the Informative References column, even as those references update over time.

Too many hurdles (real or perceived) to deploying AI often lead people to take o the path of least resistance and use AI through their own accounts (e.g., personal LLMs), increasing the risk of incidents such as data leaks.
Organizations are seeking guidance on how to answer the question, “How can o we trust an AI system before giving it our data?”
Potential options to address testing and evaluation were presented, including o performance metrics, certifications, and benchmarking.

Zero-trust and reduced trust discussions as they relate to AI decisions and o actions within an organization indicated there may be a need to treat AI similarly to how human insider threats are addressed.

AI is often deployed in organizations without an understanding of the associated o or impacted technology. Organizations must understand the technology they are deploying as well as how to securely deploy it and manage associated opportunities and risks. The notion of “shadow AI” was raised as a significant concern in the context of AI impact assessments.

From an integrity perspective, a lack of visibility into the data used to train AI o models, or into the models themselves, is a concern. This includes a lack of visibility into how AI models are trained in products and services from suppliers and third-party vendors. Participants stated that organizations need to know what data was used in a model so they can explain AI actions and functions to end users to increase the trustworthiness of AI. This includes organizational ability to communicate clearly to leadership to establish trustworthiness related to the use of AI and AI-driven decisions (whether made by AI or users informed by AI).

Considerations in the Profile should highlight the need to enhance transparency o and accountability by identifying the provenance, authenticity, and security of AI components, including open-source models and third-party dependencies.
Cryptographic signing and certification systems were suggested as additional o measures to ensure the integrity of AI systems across the supply chain.

AI supply chain documentation is important to secure the AI supply chain (e.g., o inclusion of AIBOM, similar to a Software Bill of Materials [SBOM], to address supply chain risks associated with AI systems), and to manage risks associated with open-source models and third-party dependencies and technologies.

Participants discussed whether and how to separate or designate accountability, o raising topics such as:  Clear lines of responsibility that need to exist for “developer vs. deployer vs. user” of AI systems, to include who is responsible if the systems are

deployed “out of the box” or are modified.  Concerns about the provenance of agents developed by third parties, as well as the owner and arbiter of data that is relied upon by AI systems. One of the participants offered an example of an energy company using a chatbot to respond to inquiries with safety implications, and if, in doing so, a hallucination leads to harm, the liability will fall to the energy company even if the energy company did not develop the chatbot.

Abstract

This report summarizes the discussion at the second “Cyber AI Profile Workshop,” in January 20506 during which focused on the Preliminary Draft of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework Profile for Artificial Intelligence (Cyber AI Profile). The workshop gathered input across government, industry, and academia to provide guidance for managing cybersecurity risks associated with AI systems and for leveraging AI to enhance cybersecurity capabilities to inform the next draft of the NIST Cyber AI Profile. NIST also provided an update on its work to develop the Special Publication (SP) 800-53 Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems (COSAiS). The report highlights key themes raised during the discussions, including governance challenges, stability of the Profile over time, AI attack surfaces, the need for consistent AI taxonomy, ideas for specific risk-based guidance and resources to support usability (e.g., use cases), and AI-enabled cyber defense opportunities.

1. Introduction

On January 14, 2026, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE) hosted the public workshop Cyber AI Profile Workshop #2 to gather feedback on the Preliminary Draft of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework Profile for Artificial Intelligence (Cyber AI Profile) [1] published on December 16, 2025. This document provides a summary of the workshop’s discussions, including opening remarks, panel, morning presentations, and afternoon breakout sessions. This workshop aimed to raise awareness of artificial intelligence (AI) and cybersecurity projects at NIST and obtain feedback on priority areas for organizations integrating AI into their cybersecurity infrastructure. The workshop provided a forum for stakeholders to provide input to the Cyber AI Profile, including usability, scope, content, and alignment with existing cybersecurity and AI resources. By incorporating insights from participants across various organizations, the workshop established a collaborative foundation for addressing AI-specific cybersecurity challenges while enabling organizations to harness AI’s transformative potential.
1.1. About the NIST Cyber AI Profile

Recent advances in AI technologies bring great opportunities, but also new and modified cybersecurity risks and impacts that need to be managed. NIST is extending and adapting existing frameworks, such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (CSF 2.0) [2], to assist organizations as they face these new or expanded risks. The Cyber AI Profile is being developed in response to feedback from the cybersecurity and AI communities, indicating that there would be value in guidelines based on the CSF 2.0. The community was clear that there are opportunities for using AI to enhance cybersecurity capabilities, as well as new considerations for managing cybersecurity risk related to AI systems.

Organizations vary in how they use AI. Some organizations may not yet be using AI. Some may be using cybersecurity solutions enabled with machine learning (ML) technology for pattern detection and planning but have not yet adopted newer AI capabilities, such as Generative AI (genAI) or Agentic AI. Regardless of where organizations are on their AI journey, they need risk management approaches that support the realities of advancements in AI use to position them to defend against AI-enabled cyberattacks from adversaries and to leverage AI-enabled cyber defense capabilities. To address these emerging risks and opportunities, particularly in a rapidly evolving field, NIST is developing the Cyber AI Profile [1] to identify how organizations can leverage and adapt the CSF 2.0 [2] to manage AI-related cybersecurity risks effectively. The Cyber AI Profile will seek to help organizations integrate AI-specific considerations into existing cybersecurity programs by:
Establishing a shared understanding of AI-related cybersecurity priorities and considerations for any organization;
Fostering collaboration and communication across the AI and cybersecurity communities; and
Providing common AI cybersecurity target outcomes that organizations can use to support strategic planning efforts and cybersecurity assessments, based on the CSF Core.
1.2. Background for the Cyber AI Profile Workshop #2

The workshop’s aim was to gather community feedback on the preliminary draft of the Cyber AI Profile to shape its final direction and content. By engaging stakeholders across sectors, NIST aims to ensure the development of meaningful guidelines that support organizations in managing AI-related cybersecurity risks while capitalizing on AI’s capabilities.

The preliminary draft of the Cyber AI Profile [1] is the culmination of NIST research as well as an open dialogue with the public. Building on the Cybersecurity and AI Workshop Concept Paper [3] that outlined NIST’s initial observations and proposed approaches, NIST collected additional feedback through Cyber AI Workshop #1 and the August and September 2025 Community of Interest working sessions to develop the preliminary draft. The Cyber AI Profile Workshop #2 agenda (see Table 1) and planned discussions focused on addressing open questions about the draft and on seeking additional public input.
The workshop also provided background on NIST’s portfolio of AI and cybersecurity-related projects, including the Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems (COSAiS) [4] work.

2.2. Panel: AI and Cybersecurity Projects at NIST

The panel, moderated by Ms. Barbara Cuthill, NIST Co-Lead for the Cyber AI Profile, provided an overview of a selection of NIST AI projects related to cybersecurity and highlighted how these efforts connect with the Cyber AI Profile and related NCCoE activities.

Ms. Hamin provided an overview of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) [7], which was reorganized and rechartered with a broader mission in early 2025. CAISI leads evaluations and assessments of United States (U.S.) and adversary AI systems, develops best practices and standards for improving AI security, and advances U.S. AI standards internationally. Ms. Hamin shared the activities completed to date to achieve these goals, highlighting work related to securing AI agents and agent systems and the security threats, risks, and challenges they face, which could hinder adoption and pose risks to public safety and national security. CAISI also develops voluntary practices to include automated benchmark evaluations of language models and AI agent systems [8]. Sharing such AI model evaluations on the state of model security, Ms. Hamin noted, can help consumers and decision-makers understand the relative security of these models. Ms. Hamin highlighted where CAISI continues to help improve the security of U.S. AI systems through the discovery of vulnerabilities and the development of guidelines and best practices. Ms. Hamin concluded by sharing how the community can get involved in CAISI, such as providing input on CAISI’s recently published “Request for Information Regarding Security Considerations for Artificial Intelligence Agents” [9].

Mr. Vassilev opened with an overview of areas considered part of adversarial AI, noting that trends have emerged that show a transition from static chatbots to agentic AI, which both give advice and take actions that can help automate workflows. Mr. Vassilev stated that while agentic AI can improve productivity, it simultaneously increases the attack surface available to attackers to exploit. Mr. Vassilev noted that over the last three to five years, there has been a recurring pattern where a large language model (LLM) is released and, within days of its release, reports emerge of successful attacks against that LLM. To understand why this pattern exists, Mr. Vassilev shared that NIST performed rigorous mathematical analysis on the robustness of guardrail mechanisms intended to thwart attacks on AI models. Results from this analysis led NIST to conclude that there are no guardrails universally robust enough to withstand adversarial attacks and the prompts available to jailbreak systems. Mr. Vassilev stated that to protect against such attacks, proactive adoption of adaptive defense strategies is necessary. These strategies should include continuous in-house red teaming and ongoing updates to guardrails, with the goal of discouraging adversaries by raising the threshold for the effort required to exploit LLMs. To support these strategic efforts, NIST plans to update the NIST 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations [10], to include agentic AI and the landscape of its attacks and potential mitigations to support the AI security community. Mr. Vassilev also noted the connection to the COSAiS project and this effort.

Mr. Booth provided a description of Dioptra [11], noting that it serves as a test platform that allows evaluations of different AI systems in a reproducible manner and tracks their inputs and outputs, understanding the different models and scenarios as they relate to those inputs and outputs. Mr. Booth also gave an overview of the different use cases for Dioptra, enabling individuals, based on their areas of expertise, to obtain specific insights that can inform their work. Use cases mentioned by Mr. Booth included using Dioptra to conduct testing that supports the characterization and evaluation of an AI system prior to deployment as well as using Dioptra by researchers to understand how attacks and defenses might perform relative to a new model or training technique. Mr. Booth noted that Dioptra is available on GitHub as an open-source project, is in the process of being updated to version 1.1 (both the test platform and its associated documentation), and includes new features such as built-in support for artifact handling.

Mr. Booth also gave an overview of the SSDF AI Profile (NIST SP 800-218A, Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile) [12]. Mr. Booth explained that the goal is to make the Profile broadly applicable to AI systems and to examine what is unique or new in AI system development. For example, system developers must also consider the larger scale of data used by AI systems, as well as the reliability and protection mechanisms against attacks, and data management activities such as cleaning and pre-processing. When developing AI systems, data and code must be tracked to understand what happens with data from the moment it is collected and how it is fed into training systems. Mr. Booth also noted that organizations need to be aware that reusing third-party AI models can introduce security concerns, such as providing threat vectors for adversaries to exploit NIST is assessing the timeline for updating the SSDF AI Profile published in July 2024. The SSDF [13], which serves as the basis for the SSDF AI Profile, was recently updated to version 1.2 (initial public draft [IPD]) [14], consistent with Executive Order 14306 [15]. The public comment period for the SSDF was from December 2025 to January 2026.

The PETs program conducts investigations into privacy-enhancing technologies, which are technical tools or controls intended to reduce privacy risks arising from the collection, sharing, and processing of potentially sensitive data. Mr. Howarth described the PETs program [16] as producing guidelines and frameworks to evaluate and manage privacy risks. Mr. Howarth shared that NIST is developing the PETs testbed at the NCCoE, which will include benchmark data and model test deployments to demonstrate how PETs are deployed and investigate trade-offs, with the goal of creating a comprehensive set of tools to guide organizations when selecting and deploying PETs and managing privacy risks. Mr. Howarth continued by stating that PETs programs, to include the NIST Collaborative Research Cycle (CRC) [17], are complementary to AI risk management efforts. The CRC program is the largest collection of synthetic data for benchmarking exercises related to privacy. Under the CRC program, NIST is analyzing the consequences of using and training AI/ML with synthetic data and is exploring the impacts on AI/ML performance.

Mr. Howarth spoke about a second program that is demonstrating how to apply privacy-preserving federated learning (PPFL). Federated learning connects ML among unconnected devices, enabling increases to both compute power and the amount of data available to train ML algorithms. PPFL introduces important privacy considerations, which NIST’s privacy-preserving federated learning platform is being used to investigate. NIST is asking questions about how different privatization mechanisms affect ML performance and which security and privacy controls are needed. NIST plans to publish model code as well as a complementary privacy and cybersecurity threat modeling example that shows the types of threats that PPFL is attempting to manage and applicable privacy and cybersecurity controls. Mr. Howarth concluded by noting that reducing privacy threats requires a strong cybersecurity foundation and emphasized that using synthetic data alone does not adequately protect privacy unless the original data is also secured.

Mr. Galluzzo opened by acknowledging that AI agents are starting to change the context and conversation around traditional cybersecurity controls, including regarding issues on agent access and identifying agents operating in organizations, how to authenticate an agent and verify it is what it claims to be, and how to authorize and manage access on an ongoing basis for agents to engage with data or take particular action, such as accessing data or resources, and necessary restrictions on those actions to address concerns that may result from data aggregation.

The Agent Identities work focuses on understanding and creating authorization flows and delegations pertaining to created agents, specifically determining the individual(s) who will be accountable for actions the AI system may take and how to bind the identity of that individual to the actions the agent is taking so organizations can audit, log, and understand the chains of trust related to agent actions. This work also considers human-in-the-loop scenarios, such as specifying who is notified and who decides whether to grant access when an agent tries to access data it is not authorized to use. Mr. Galluzzo concluded by noting that it is important to understand the balance between the benefits of agents operating within an enterprise and the need to protect the information an agent might access to preserve privacy, security, and confidentiality, to help inform where adaptations may be needed.

NIST is planning to propose an NCCoE collaboration project through an initial concept paper based on use cases, including how to deploy agents at scale, with the goal of launching an NCCoE demonstration project that includes industry involvement.

Mr. Lee opened with an overview of the NCCoE Chatbot [20], stating that the Chatbot was designed to increase the efficiency and ease of conducting searches on the wealth of information the NCCoE has available on its website. The NCCoE Chatbot uses a customized retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based LLM to assist with searching large amounts of data. The customized RAG-LLM includes a metadata layer designed to “filter down” the search index, focusing on specific keywords or information before the Chatbot conducts a semantic similarity vector comparison to produce its search results. Mr. Lee noted that including the metadata layer in the Chatbot is intended to address the lag in responses that occurs as the search index grows.

Mr. Lee shared that NIST Interagency Report (IR) 8579 (IPD), “Developing the NCCoE Chatbot: Technical and Security Learnings from the Initial Implementation” [21], provides information on the NCCoE Chatbot as well as security considerations when developing prompts to support trust. NIST IR 8579 also includes details on the reasoning behind the types of metadata information used in metadata indexing and filtering.

The panelists also discussed the importance that NIST places on collaboration across programs. For example, there are collaboration touchpoints between the NCCoE agent identity work and the CAISI agent work. NIST also develops guidelines, such as the Cyber AI Profile, that provide a high-level understanding of cybersecurity outcomes and objectives and specific recommendations on how to achieve them, using, for example, COSAiS for specific AI types.

Moving to the discussion on the Emerging Technology Accelerators, Dr. Schlenoff mentioned the December 2025 establishment of the “AI Accelerator,” [22] which will include the “AI Economic Security Center for U.S. Manufacturing Productivity” and the “AI Economic Security Center to Secure U.S. Critical Infrastructure from Cyberthreats.” Dr. Schlenoff provided overviews of each of these areas in the AI Accelerator. Dr. Schlenoff noted that there are opportunities to involve academia, whether during pre-standardization development (e.g., participation in research that will inform the standards) or during standard development (e.g., through standards bodies). NIST is working with academic partners but is open to exploring increased engagement and involvement.
